newsitem.title: UK: Maverick Leigh hails Oscar nomination triumph.
newsitem.headline: Maverick Leigh hails Oscar nomination triumph.

text.p: Director Mike Leigh, maverick master of improvisation, on Tuesday hailed the five Oscar nominations for his "Secrets and Lies" as a welcome shot in the arm for the British film industry.
"As ever, one has made a film without compromising," said the director of quirky tales about drab suburban life that have captured the imagination of audiences around the world.

Leigh, 53, who starts with a blank page and spends months honing the script with his actors, told Reuters: "I am thrilled and delighted and surprised. The main thing is that Americans are looking beyond Hollywood."

He was nominated as best director for "Secrets and Lies", his harrowing tale of a young black woman's search for her natural mother. It was also nominated as best film and Brenda Blethyn was picked in the Best Actress category.
Leigh was particularly delighted that his offbeat technique was rewarded with an original screenplay nomination.
"I work up the screenplay with the actors. It involves much improvisation. This makes it all worthwhile."
Leigh, whose first film "Bleak Moments" in 1971 was financed by actor Albert Finney, has refused to pander to mainstream audiences.

"We were not tailoring it for the American market but it speaks to people right across the board. People laughed and cried everywhere," he said. "The film has crossed over and got to audiences who had not been able to see my stuff."
Leigh first tasted international success in 1993 when his "Naked" won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film festival. He repeated that feat with "Secrets and Lies".

His biggest success ran true to form. The actors worked for nine months on a film known only as "Untitled 95". With no script and no plot, he gradually built up the story in collaboration with his players.

Blethyn said she revelled in the challenge: "We built the character from infancy, the geography of where she was born, her little idiosyncrasies -- childhood injuries, how obedient she was, her sense of smell, the minutest detail."
Leigh never sought Hollywood's approval but now will be under the international spotlight next month in what is still the centre of world cinema.

The director, described by one critic as "an artist who entertains while hitting wher it hurts," clearly revelled in the irony. "To win five nominations is overwhelming. This really is a shot in the arm for British cinema."
